opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a lot that's appealing about it. The core intuition Yann has, that you shouldn't be trying to predict every pixel, seems basically right to me. Much of the visual world is noise from the point of view of understanding. The exact texture of leaves blowing in the wind, or the precise pattern of light on water, isn't something an intelligent agent needs to reconstruct. So predicting in an abstract representation space, rather than in raw pixel space, is a very sensible idea. It's closer to what we believe humans do: we're forming expectations about objects, their positions, how things will move. We're not hallucinating a high-resolution movie in our heads.

Coming from language, I find this interesting, because in some sense language got lucky. Words are already a fairly abstract, discrete, human-designed representation. When you do next-token prediction on text, you're already predicting at a semantic level, and that's part of why it has worked so remarkably well. Vision doesn't come pre-packaged that way, so you need some way to learn the abstraction, and JEPA is one principled attempt at doing that.

That said, I'd have a couple of reservations. One is the empirical question: so far, the joint-embedding approaches have produced good representations, but they haven't yet produced the kind of dramatic, obviously general capabilities we've seen from large generative models. Generative pretraining, for all its supposed inefficiency, has the virtue of a very clear, dense training signal, and it scales in a predictable way. With joint-embedding methods, you're always fighting things like representation collapse, and the field has needed a lot of clever tricks to keep the objective well behaved.

The other reservation is a bit more philosophical. Yann tends to frame this as an either-or, that autoregressive generative models are a dead end and this is the way forward. I'm more of a pluralist. I suspect the eventual systems will combine things: some generative modeling, some prediction in latent space, and grounding through interaction with the world, not just passively watching video. Learning a good world model probably requires an agent that acts and sees the consequences of its actions, and that's a piece that's still largely missing from most of this work.

So overall, I think it's a valuable and well-motivated research direction, and it's good that someone with Yann's influence is pushing hard on an alternative to the dominant paradigm. But I'd say the jury's still out on whether it will be *the* answer, rather than one important ingredient.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the jury is still out on whether JEPA will be “the” answer, framing it instead as potentially one important ingredient.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the core intuition behind JEPA is a good one, and it's not really a new one. The idea is that you shouldn't be predicting every pixel. If you're trying to build a model of the visual world, most of what's in an image or a video is noise from the point of view of what you actually want to understand. The exact pattern of leaves on a tree, the precise texture of a carpet, those aren't things a system needs to reconstruct to know what's going on in a scene. So the move to say, let's predict in a learned representation space rather than in the raw input space, that's sensible. People in the self-supervised learning world had been circling that idea for a while with things like BYOL and the contrastive methods, and JEPA is in some ways a cleaner, more principled framing of it.

Where I'd be a bit more cautious is in how strongly Yann sometimes positions it. He's argued fairly forcefully that this is the path to real world models and that autoregressive, generative approaches are something of a dead end. And I just don't think the evidence supports that strong a claim yet. The results on things like I-JEPA and V-JEPA are respectable, you get good representations with less compute than some alternatives, but they haven't been transformative in the way that, say, scaling language models was. Meanwhile, the generative approaches that he's been skeptical of, the video diffusion models and so on, have made remarkable progress, and they do seem to be learning quite a lot about physical structure almost as a byproduct of being forced to generate.

The other thing I'd flag, coming at this from the language side, is that there's a persistent question about what the representation is actually capturing. In language, we have a natural discrete structure that gives you some leverage. In vision, when you learn an abstract latent space, you have to worry about collapse, you have to worry about whether the predictor is learning something genuinely semantic or something that happens to be easy to predict. JEPA addresses that with various architectural tricks, but it's still a bit of an open question whether you get the kind of rich, compositional understanding of scenes that we'd actually want.

So my honest assessment is that it's a serious, thoughtful research direction that deserves attention, and it's probably right in spirit that the eventual solution involves prediction at some level of abstraction above pixels. But I'd be surprised if it turns out to be the one true path, and I'd be especially surprised if it works entirely in isolation from the generative and language-conditioned approaches that are showing so much momentum right now. My guess is the eventual systems will be hybrids, and some of JEPA's ideas will be in there, but so will a lot of other things.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the evidence does not support treating JEPA as the path to real world models, and doubts it will be the “one true path.”

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction. One of the central questions in learning from vision is what you should try to predict. If you predict every pixel, you’re spending a lot of effort on details that may be unpredictable or irrelevant to understanding what’s happening. With JEPA, the idea is to predict in a learned representation space, where you can hopefully capture the important structure without having to reconstruct every detail of the image.

That seems like a sensible approach to learning about the visual world. But a lot depends on what that representation preserves. You want it to abstract away irrelevant detail while retaining the information you’ll need to understand objects, actions, and their consequences. Getting that balance right is a substantial part of the problem.

So I’m enthusiastic about exploring it. I’m less convinced that we already know that this is the route to a sufficiently rich world model, or that it establishes that generative approaches are fundamentally misguided. The interesting test is what these systems can learn and then use to make predictions in new situations.

r001.rationale: The response says it is not convinced JEPA is already known to be the route to a sufficiently rich world model, communicating that it has not been established as the best approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very interesting direction. One of the big questions in learning from the visual world is what you should try to predict. If you predict every pixel, you’re spending an enormous amount of effort modeling details that may not matter for understanding or acting: the precise texture of a surface, or how the leaves on a tree happen to move.

The idea behind JEPA is to predict in a learned representation space, where you can hopefully capture the underlying structure without having to reconstruct all those details. That seems like a very sensible thing to explore.

But the difficult question is what makes that representation capture the right things. You want it to retain information about objects, their relationships, and how the world changes, while discarding genuinely irrelevant variation. Simply moving prediction into a representation space doesn’t automatically solve that problem.

So I’m sympathetic to the direction. I’m less convinced that we already know it’s the route to a sufficiently rich world model, or that it establishes that generative approaches are a dead end. Those are questions we should settle by seeing what these models can learn and do.

r001.rationale: The response says it is not convinced JEPA is already known to be the route to a sufficiently rich world model, communicating that it has not been established as the best approach.
